claim: H3K9me2 marks only peripheral heterochromatin in murine NIH/3T3 fibroblasts.
source: Immunostaining of murine NIH/3T3 fibroblasts for repressive histone modifications demonstrates the distribution of the major types of heterochromatin in the nucleus of a single cell (Figure 1a). H3K9me2 marks only peripheral heterochromatin, whereas H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 co-localize with heterochromatin in the nuclear interior, or at both the interior and the periphery (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1a and described in the text.

claim: H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 co-localize with heterochromatin in the nuclear interior, or at both the interior and the periphery.
source: H3K9me2 marks only peripheral heterochromatin, whereas H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 co-localize with heterochromatin in the nuclear interior, or at both the interior and the periphery (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K9me2 signal is closely associated with the nuclear lamina marker Lamin B in single cell immunostaining.
source: The close association between H3K9me2 and the nuclear lamina marker Lamin B in single cell immunostaining is consistent with the correlation between H3K9me2 and Lamin B ChIP-seq data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by single cell immunostaining and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K9me2 chromatin is adjacent to the nuclear lamina as verified by super-resolution microscopy.
source: The adjacency of H3K9me2 chromatin to the nuclear lamina was verified by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Stochastic Optical Reconstruction Microscopy (STORM) using Voronoi tessellation confirms a non-random distribution of the H3K9me2 signal at the periphery of the nucleus.
source: Stochastic Optical Reconstruction Microscopy (STORM) using a Voronoi tessellation confirms a non-random distribution of the H3K9me2 signal at the periphery of the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by STORM imaging and Voronoi tessellation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Restriction of H3K9me2-marked heterochromatin to the nuclear periphery is evolutionarily conserved from C. elegans to humans.
source: We further examined H3K9me2-marked heterochromatin across species and observe that restriction to the nuclear periphery is evolutionarily conserved from C. elegans to humans (Figure 1c) suggesting functional significance of the localization of this histone post-translational modification.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data across multiple species shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The anti-H3K9me2 antibody detects only the dimethyl modification and only on lysine 9 of histone H3.
source: By preincubating the anti-H3K9me2 antibody with peptides representing each of the possible histone tail modifications before use in immunostaining, we were able to determine that the H3K9me2 antibody detects only the dimethyl modification and only on lysine 9 of histone H3 (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by peptide blocking experiments shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking the H3K9me2 antibody with an H3K9me2 peptide allows the specific signal observed at the nuclear periphery to be distinguished from non-specific background signal observed in the nuclear interior.
source: Additionally, by blocking the H3K9me2 antibody with an H3K9me2 peptide, the specific signal observed at the nuclear periphery can be distinguished from non-specific background signal observed in the nuclear interior and detected with signal intensity analysis (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by antibody blocking and signal intensity analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: STORM imaging confirms that blocking the H3K9me2 antibody with an H3K9me2 peptide distinguishes specific peripheral signal from non-specific background.
source: This observation was further confirmed by STORM imaging (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: H3K9me2 is necessary for peripheral localization of chromatin.
source: Given the specificity of H3K9me2 for peripheral heterochromatin, we hypothesized that this epigenetic histone modification is necessary for peripheral localization of chromatin and might be recognized by a nuclear peripheral protein 'reader' to tether chromatin to the nuclear lamina (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on the specificity of H3K9me2 for peripheral heterochromatin.

claim: CEC-4 functions as a reader of methylated H3K9 and is localized to the nuclear periphery in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, CEC-4 functions as a reader of methylated H3K9 and is localized to the nuclear periphery where it is thought to function as part of a tethering complex for peripheral heterochromatin (Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015.

claim: CEC-4 is required for peripheral heterochromatin anchoring in C. elegans.
source: Since CEC-4 is required for peripheral heterochromatin anchoring (Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015), we compared the localization of H3K9me2 in wild-type and cec-4-null embryo cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015.

claim: H3K9me2 is no longer restricted to the periphery in cec-4-null C. elegans embryo cells.
source: Immunostaining revealed a dramatic alteration in spatial patterning in which H3K9me2 is no longer restricted to the periphery in cec-4-null cells (Figure 3b and c, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3b and c.

claim: Localization of H3K9me2-marked chromatin at the nuclear lamina is restored by expression of the CEC-4-mCherry transgene in cec-4-null C. elegans.
source: Localization of the H3K9me2-marked chromatin at the nuclear lamina was restored by expression of the CEC-4-mCherry transgene (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of CEC-4 does not affect H3K9me3 localization in C. elegans embryo cells.
source: Despite previous observations of CEC-4 binding to all methylated forms of H3K9 in vitro (Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015), in vivo loss of CEC-4 does not affect H3K9me3 localization. H3K9me3 is found both at the nuclear periphery and in the nucleoplasm, but its localization does not vary between wide-type and cec-4-null embryo cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of CEC-4 results in a specific effect on H3K9me2-marked chromatin and not H3K9me3-marked chromatin.
source: These data suggest loss of a peripheral heterochromatin tether, CEC-4, results in a specific effect on H3K9me2-marked chromatin and not H3K9me3-marked chromatin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing differential effects on H3K9me2 vs H3K9me3 localization upon CEC-4 loss.

claim: Wild-type GFP-H3 is observed throughout the nucleus including at the nuclear periphery, where it overlaps with endogenous H3K9me2 staining, immediately adjacent to Lamin B.
source: Wild-type GFP-H3 was observed throughout the nucleus including at the nuclear periphery, where it overlapped with endogenous H3K9me2 staining, immediately adjacent to Lamin B (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: GFP-H3K9A and GFP-H3K9E fail to partition to the nuclear periphery.
source: In contrast, GFP-H3K9A and GFP-H3K9E failed to partition to the nuclear periphery (Figure 3d–f, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3d–f.

claim: Dimethylation of H3K9 is required for either incorporation into peripheral nucleosomes, or for retention within nucleosomes at the periphery.
source: Given that wild-type GFP-H3 is incorporated and observed at the nuclear periphery, we interpret the inability of the K9A and K9E mutants to partition to the periphery to suggest that lysine nine dimethylation is required for either incorporation into peripheral nucleosomes, or for retention within nucleosomes at the periphery.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that K9A and K9E mutants fail to localize to the periphery.

claim: Dimethylation of H3K9 orchestrates positioning of chromatin to the nuclear periphery.
source: Combined with the CEC-4 results, this indicates that dimethylation of H3K9 orchestrates positioning of chromatin to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of CEC-4 experiments and H3 mutant experiments.

claim: H3S10 phosphorylation is associated with mitotic chromosome condensation.
source: H3S10 phosphorylation is associated with mitotic chromosome condensation (Wei et al., 1999; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003) and, together with the neighboring Lys9 residue, has been proposed to function as a 'phospho-methyl switch' to modulate binding of H3 to effector proteins (Varier et al., 2010; Fischle et al., 2003; Wang and Higgins, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei et al., 1999; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003.

claim: H3S10 and H3K9 have been proposed to function as a 'phospho-methyl switch' to modulate binding of H3 to effector proteins.
source: H3S10 phosphorylation is associated with mitotic chromosome condensation (Wei et al., 1999; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003) and, together with the neighboring Lys9 residue, has been proposed to function as a 'phospho-methyl switch' to modulate binding of H3 to effector proteins (Varier et al., 2010; Fischle et al., 2003; Wang and Higgins, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Varier et al., 2010; Fischle et al., 2003; Wang and Higgins, 2013.

claim: GFP-H3S10E is distributed throughout the nucleus, but not at the nuclear periphery.
source: Expression of a GFP-tagged H3 mutant in which Ser10 is replaced with the phospho-mimic glutamic acid (H3S10E) resulted in distribution of the GFP-H3S10E throughout the nucleus, but notably not at the nuclear periphery (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3d–f.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser10 can prevent H3 peripheral localization.
source: This is consistent with the ability of phosphorylated Ser10 to inhibit interaction of the reader with H3K9me2 and suggests that phosphorylation of Ser10 can prevent H3 peripheral localization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the H3S10E mutant data.

claim: H3S10A produces a pattern similar to wild-type GFP-H3 in interphase cells.
source: Replacement of H3 Ser10 with an alanine (H3S10A) precludes phosphorylation at this site and did not disrupt peripheral localization. Instead, H3S10A produced a pattern similar to wild-type GFP-H3 in interphase cells (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3d–f.

claim: H3K9me2 is required for localization of heterochromatin to the nuclear periphery.
source: Together, these H3 mutant results suggest that H3K9me2 is required for localization of heterochromatin to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the H3 mutant experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser10 can prevent or disrupt association of heterochromatin with the nuclear periphery as part of a phospho-methyl switch.
source: Further, they indicate that phosphorylation of Ser10 can prevent or disrupt this association as part of a phospho-methyl switch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the H3 mutant experiments.

claim: CEC-4 binds methylated H3K9 peptides and this binding is reduced by 2 orders of magnitude if the adjacent Ser10 is phosphorylated.
source: Indeed, experimental results from the Gasser lab demonstrated that CEC-4 binds methylated H3K9 peptides and this binding is reduced by 2 orders of magnitude if the adjacent Ser10 is phosphorylated (Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015.

claim: H3K9me2 persists on mitotic chromatin.
source: Examination of cells progressing through the consecutive phases of mitosis revealed persistence of H3K9me2 on mitotic chromatin (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prior to disassembly of the nuclear lamina in prophase, H3K9me2-marked chromatin begins to detach from the nuclear periphery.
source: Prior to disassembly of the nuclear lamina in prophase, H3K9me2-marked chromatin begins to detach from the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser10 on the H3 tail adjacent to dimethylated Lys9 (H3K9me2S10p) begins in prophase and persists until late telophase.
source: Concordant with this detachment, we observe phosphorylation of Ser10 on the H3 tail adjacent to dimethylated Lys9 (H3K9me2S10p) beginning in prophase and persisting until late telophase (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: The anti-H3K9me2S10p antibody does not recognize the H3K9me2 epitope without an adjacent phosphate group on S10, nor does it recognize H3S10p alone.
source: Similar to the anti-H3K9me2 antibody (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we carefully tested the specificity of the anti-H3K9me2S10p antibody used in these experiments and verified that it does not recognize the H3K9me2 epitope without an adjacent phosphate group on S10, nor does it recognize H3S10p alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by antibody specificity testing shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: H3S10 phosphorylation in prophase may contribute to release of H3K9me2 readers/tethers and detachment from the nuclear periphery.
source: H3S10 phosphorylation in prophase may contribute to release of H3K9me2 readers/tethers (Eberlin et al., 2008; Hirota et al., 2005) and detachment from the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Eberlin et al., 2008; Hirota et al., 2005.

claim: Not every histone H3 Ser10 adjacent to H3K9me2 is phosphorylated during mitosis.
source: Our data suggest that not every histone H3 Ser10 adjacent to H3K9me2 is phosphorylated since we observe some overlap of staining with the H3K9me2 and H3K9me2S10p antibodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunostaining data showing overlap of H3K9me2 and H3K9me2S10p signals.

claim: Re-establishment of the H3K9me2 layer occurs in parallel with reassembly of the nuclear lamina as telophase progresses.
source: We also examined cells at successive points in telophase. As telophase progresses, re-establishment of the H3K9me2 layer occurs in parallel with reassembly of the nuclear lamina. We observed aggregation of H3K9me2-marked chromatin and the reformation of this heterochromatin layer at the interface with the newly forming nuclear lamina structure (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Chromatin marked with H3K9me2S10p is not enriched at the interface of the forming nuclear lamina but remains in the nucleoplasm.
source: However, chromatin marked with H3K9me2S10p was not enriched at the interface of the forming nuclear lamina but remained in the nucleoplasm (Figure 4d), suggesting that loss of S10 phosphorylation occurs prior to association of chromatin with the nuclear lamina.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Loss of S10 phosphorylation occurs prior to association of chromatin with the nuclear lamina.
source: However, chromatin marked with H3K9me2S10p was not enriched at the interface of the forming nuclear lamina but remained in the nucleoplasm (Figure 4d), suggesting that loss of S10 phosphorylation occurs prior to association of chromatin with the nuclear lamina.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunostaining data showing H3K9me2S10p in the nucleoplasm during telophase.

claim: Little or no H3K9me2S10p is detected in daughter cells after mitosis is complete.
source: We detected little or no H3K9me2S10p in daughter cells after mitosis was complete (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: H3K9me3 is enriched in microsatellite heterochromatin and persists through mitosis.
source: A subset of H3K9me3-marked chromatin is at the nuclear periphery, though it is not restricted to the periphery as is H3K9me2. H3K9me3 is enriched in microsatellite heterochromatin and persists through mitosis (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In telophase, there are strong differences in localization of H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and H3K4me3 in contrast to H3K9me2.
source: In addition, in telophase we noted strong differences in localization of other repressive (H3K9me3, H3K27me3) and active (H3K4me3) histone marks in contrast to H3K9me2 (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: H3K9me3 chromatin is not enriched at the interface with the forming nuclear lamina during telophase and mitotic exit.
source: Trimethylated H3K9 is also distinct from H3K9me2 in that H3K9me3 chromatin is not enriched at the interface with the forming nuclear lamina during telophase and mitotic exit.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining data.

claim: In newly formed daughter cells, H3K9me2- but not H3K9me3-marked chromatin is preferentially associated with the nuclear lamina.
source: In the newly formed daughter cells, we observed H3K9me2- but not H3K9me3-marked chromatin preferentially associated with the nuclear lamina.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining data.

claim: An average of 82% of LAD probes (74–90% in individual cells) were positioned at the nuclear periphery within the measured thickness of the H3K9me2 chromatin layer in interphase cells.
source: In a population of interphase cells, we found the LAD probes to be at the periphery of individual nuclei at a frequency consistent with previous observations of haploid cells in studies using single-cell DamID (Kind et al., 2015). An average of 82% of LAD probes (74–90% in individual cells) were positioned at the nuclear periphery within the measured thickness of the H3K9me2 chromatin layer in interphase cells (Figure 6a, Video 1, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by oligopaint FISH data shown in Figure 6a and Video 1, and citation to Kind et al., 2015.

claim: An average of 89% of non-LAD probes (79–95% in individual cells) segregated outside of the peripheral chromatin layer in interphase cells.
source: Non-LAD probes, assessed in each of the same interphase cells, were more frequently found in the nucleoplasm, as expected: an average of 89% of non-LAD probes (79–95% in individual cells) segregated outside of the peripheral chromatin layer (Figure 6a, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by oligopaint FISH data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Both LAD and non-LAD probes are present at similar distances from the DNA surface in cells in metaphase.
source: Next, we examined the location of these pools of representative LAD and non-LAD genomic loci in cells undergoing mitosis. Both LAD and non-LAD probes are present at similar distances from the DNA surface in cells in metaphase, a point in mitosis at which the nuclear lamina has disassembled (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Video 2, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by oligopaint FISH data shown in Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and Video 2.

claim: By telophase, LAD probes have repositioned to the nuclear periphery.
source: However, by telophase, LAD probes have repositioned to the nuclear periphery (Figure 6c, Video 3, Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that H3K9me2-marked domains that were at the periphery in parent cells are specifically repositioned at the periphery in daughter nuclei before mitotic exit.
evidence: Supported by oligopaint FISH data shown in Figure 6c and Video 3.

claim: H3K9me2-marked domains that were at the periphery in parent cells are specifically repositioned at the periphery in daughter nuclei before mitotic exit.
source: However, by telophase, LAD probes have repositioned to the nuclear periphery (Figure 6c, Video 3, Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that H3K9me2-marked domains that were at the periphery in parent cells are specifically repositioned at the periphery in daughter nuclei before mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oligopaint FISH data showing LAD repositioning to the periphery by telophase.

claim: In telophase, non-LAD probes remained largely in the nucleoplasm, away from the nuclear lamina.
source: In these same cells in telophase, non-LAD probes remained largely in the nucleoplasm, away from the nuclear lamina (Figure 6c, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by oligopaint FISH data shown in Figure 6c and Video 3.

claim: Specific LADs found at the nuclear periphery in parental cells are repositioned at the periphery at mitotic exit.
source: Thus, specific LADs found at the nuclear periphery in parental cells are repositioned at the periphery at mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oligopaint FISH data.

claim: H3K9me2 marks chromatin domains that are specifically positioned at the nuclear lamina during interphase.
source: Our results provide experimental support of a model for nuclear peripheral localization and mitotic inheritance of lamina-associated heterochromatin (Figure 7). We show that H3K9me2 marks chromatin domains that are specifically positioned at the nuclear lamina during interphase.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: In mitosis, H3K9me2-marked domains retain and are bookmarked by H3K9me2.
source: In mitosis, these domains retain and are bookmarked by H3K9me2.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: H3S10 phosphorylation promotes release of H3K9me2-marked chromatin from the nuclear periphery, likely by masking the Lys9 dimethyl modification from recognition by its reader/tether.
source: H3S10 phosphorylation promotes release from the nuclear periphery, likely by masking the Lys9 dimethyl modification from recognition by its reader/tether (Fischle et al., 2003; Wang and Higgins, 2013; Eberlin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript, supported by citations to Fischle et al., 2003; Wang and Higgins, 2013; Eberlin et al., 2008.

claim: In late stages of mitosis, dephosphorylation of H3S10 unmasks bookmarked LADs which are then reassembled at the nuclear periphery during nuclear lamina reformation in the nuclei of daughter cells.
source: In late stages of mitosis, dephosphorylation of H3S10 unmasks bookmarked LADs which are then reassembled at the nuclear periphery during nuclear lamina reformation in the nuclei of daughter cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The H3K9me2 modification of peripheral heterochromatin ensures that positional information is safeguarded through cell division such that individual LADs are re-established at the nuclear periphery in daughter nuclei.
source: The H3K9me2 modification of peripheral heterochromatin ensures that positional information is safeguarded through cell division such that individual LADs are re-established at the nuclear periphery in daughter nuclei.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: H3K9me2 acts as a 3D architectural mitotic guidepost.
source: Thus, H3K9me2 acts as a 3D architectural mitotic guidepost.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The data establish a mechanism for epigenetic memory and inheritance of spatial organization of the genome.
source: Our data establish a mechanism for epigenetic memory and inheritance of spatial organization of the genome.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial arrangement of the genome inside the nucleus contributes to regulation of cell-fate choices and differentiation.
source: It is well appreciated that the spatial arrangement of the genome inside the nucleus contributes to regulation of cell-fate choices and differentiation (Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013.

claim: The mechanistic underpinnings of how the blueprint for cell-type-specific nuclear architecture is transmitted from mother to daughter cells remain poorly understood.
source: However, the mechanistic underpinnings of how the blueprint for cell-type-specific nuclear architecture is transmitted from mother to daughter cells in order to maintain cell identity remain poorly understood (Dekker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dekker et al., 2017.

claim: Separation of transcriptionally active and inactive chromatin in three-dimensional space reinforces efficient regulation of gene expression and maintains silencing of heterochromatic loci.
source: Separation of transcriptionally active and inactive chromatin in three-dimensional space reinforces efficient regulation of gene expression and maintains silencing of heterochromatic loci (reviewed in Andrey and Mundlos, 2017; Buchwalter et al., 2019; Amendola and van Steensel, 2014; Bickmore, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andrey and Mundlos, 2017; Buchwalter et al., 2019; Amendola and van Steensel, 2014; Bickmore, 2013.

claim: Aberrant gene expression patterns occur upon disruption of topological domains and, in extreme cases, are associated with oncogenic transformation.
source: This is illustrated by examples of aberrant gene expression patterns that occur upon disruption of topological domains and, in extreme cases, are associated with oncogenic transformation (Andrey and Mundlos, 2017; Flavahan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andrey and Mundlos, 2017; Flavahan et al., 2016.

claim: Lamina-associated domains (LADs) encompass approximately 30–40% of the genome.
source: Heterochromatin is segregated into spatially distinct subnuclear compartments including peripherally located lamina-associated domains (LADs) (Guelen et al., 2008), which encompass approximately 30–40% of the genome (Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010; Poleshko et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guelen et al., 2008; Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010; Poleshko et al., 2017.

claim: Proper positioning of LADs contributes to cell-type-specific gene expression in mammalian cell types.
source: Multiple examples in mammalian cell types indicate that proper positioning of LADs contributes to cell-type-specific gene expression (Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010; Poleshko et al., 2017; Robson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010; Poleshko et al., 2017; Robson et al., 2016.

claim: In Drosophila, competence of neuroblasts to respond to inductive signals depends upon stage-specific reorganization of peripheral heterochromatin.
source: Likewise, in Drosophila, competence of neuroblasts to respond to inductive signals depends upon stage-specific reorganization of peripheral heterochromatin (Kohwi et al., 2013), and muscle differentiation in Caenorhabditis elegans requires anchoring of heterochromatin to the nuclear periphery (Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohwi et al., 2013.

claim: Muscle differentiation in Caenorhabditis elegans requires anchoring of heterochromatin to the nuclear periphery.
source: Likewise, in Drosophila, competence of neuroblasts to respond to inductive signals depends upon stage-specific reorganization of peripheral heterochromatin (Kohwi et al., 2013), and muscle differentiation in Caenorhabditis elegans requires anchoring of heterochromatin to the nuclear periphery (Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Sandoval et al., 2015.

claim: Many developmental and lineage-specific genes reside in LADs.
source: These findings, combined with the observation that many developmental and lineage-specific genes reside in LADs, suggest a key role for peripheral heterochromatin in establishment and maintenance of cellular identity (Zullo et al., 2012; Poleshko et al., 2017; Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zullo et al., 2012; Poleshko et al., 2017; Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010.

claim: Peripheral heterochromatin plays a key role in establishment and maintenance of cellular identity.
source: These findings, combined with the observation that many developmental and lineage-specific genes reside in LADs, suggest a key role for peripheral heterochromatin in establishment and maintenance of cellular identity (Zullo et al., 2012; Poleshko et al., 2017; Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited studies.

claim: LADs are defined by their interaction with the nuclear lamina which is disassembled during cell division.
source: LADs are defined by their interaction with the nuclear lamina which is disassembled during cell division, posing a conundrum as to how cell-type specific LADs are remembered through mitosis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about LADs and the nuclear lamina.

claim: There does not appear to be a clear targeting sequence that localizes areas of the genome to the nuclear periphery.
source: For example, there does not appear to be a clear targeting sequence that localizes areas of the genome to the nuclear periphery (Zullo et al., 2012; Meuleman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zullo et al., 2012; Meuleman et al., 2013.

claim: Histone post-translational modifications have been implicated in LAD regulation.
source: However, histone post-translational modifications have been implicated in LAD regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of histone modifications in LAD regulation.

claim: Proline Rich Protein 14 (PRR14) recognizes H3K9me3 through an interaction with HP1.
source: Proline Rich Protein 14 (PRR14) has been shown to recognize H3K9me3, found on both peripheral and nucleoplasmic heterochromatin, through an interaction with HP1 (Poleshko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poleshko et al., 2013.

claim: There is a specific enrichment for H3K9me2 at the nuclear periphery.
source: In addition, work from our group and others has demonstrated a specific enrichment for H3K9me2 at the nuclear periphery, raising the possibility of a regulatory role in LAD positioning (Poleshko et al., 2017; Kind et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poleshko et al., 2017; Kind et al., 2013.

claim: CEC-4 is required for peripheral heterochromatin anchoring but not transcriptional repression in C. elegans.
source: Depletion studies using RNAi and loss-of-function mutants demonstrated that CEC-4 is required for peripheral heterochromatin anchoring but not transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of CEC-4 based on depletion studies.

claim: Entry into mitosis involves eviction of proteins, including RNA polymerase and many transcription factors, and reorganization of chromosomes into their characteristic metaphase form.
source: Entry into mitosis involves eviction of proteins, including RNA polymerase and many transcription factors, and reorganization of chromosomes into their characteristic metaphase form (Naumova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Naumova et al., 2013.

claim: At mitotic exit, cell-type-specific chromatin architecture, transcription factor binding, and gene expression are re-established.
source: Remarkably, at mitotic exit, cell-type-specific chromatin architecture, transcription factor binding, and gene expression are re-established (reviewed in Oomen and Dekker, 2017; Palozola et al., 2019; Hsiung and Blobel, 2016; Probst et al., 2009; Festuccia et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oomen and Dekker, 2017; Palozola et al., 2019; Hsiung and Blobel, 2016; Probst et al., 2009; Festuccia et al., 2017.

claim: Pioneering studies in the 1980s revealed the necessity for DNA in the process of nuclear lamina reassembly after mitosis.
source: Pioneering studies in the 1980 s revealed the necessity for DNA in the process of nuclear lamina reassembly after mitosis, and the activity of kinases and phosphatases were implicated in mediating interactions between lamin and chromosomes (Foisner and Gerace, 1993; Newport, 1987; Burke and Gerace, 1986; Gerace and Blobel, 1980), although the mechanistic explanation for the dependence of reassembly on chromatin has been unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Foisner and Gerace, 1993; Newport, 1987; Burke and Gerace, 1986; Gerace and Blobel, 1980.

claim: The H3K9me2 modification of nuclear lamina-associated heterochromatin, revealed upon dephosphorylation of H3S10 at mitotic exit, provides a 3D spatial guidepost for genomic regions that are to be re-localized to the nuclear periphery following mitosis.
source: Here, we utilize high resolution, single-cell imaging and oligopaints to simultaneously track 82 LAD and non-LAD genomic loci through mitosis. We show that the H3K9me2 modification of nuclear lamina-associated heterochromatin, revealed upon dephosphorylation of H3S10 at mitotic exit, provides a 3D spatial guidepost for genomic regions that are to be re-localized to the nuclear periphery following mitosis and that the nuclear lamina of daughter cells reassembles around the exposed H3K9me2 mark.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.
